Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-prompt-long-0032", "row_sha256": "c63d5e63969a19230e794d623dd3c3b034c4a2b2f65647c7637e3979a0b25949", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
okay, help me turn this into a clear request for a planning recommendation for the North Quad Film Society. We’re putting on a screening of the independent documentary The Last Orchard on Thursday, October 24. It’s for current students and staff, and we are hoping for about 70 people. We have permission to screen the film, and the filmmaker has sent a short recorded introduction, but we have not decided whether to play it before the film or save it for the discussion afterward. The request should ask for a practical plan for the event, not a general essay about running a film society. It needs to use the details below and not fill in facts we haven’t got.

There are a few options and decisions tangled up in my notes. The usual room, Cedar Hall 104, seats 64, has a projector and speakers that the society already knows how to use. The library has offered the smaller screening room, which seats 48 and has better sound, but the library coordinator has not confirmed whether its late opening is possible. We’ve also asked the student union about using its auditorium, which seats 110; it has a microphone and projector, though we have not tested either one. The union has not replied about the room yet. The society can pay up to $180 for event costs from its current allocation. That is the available total, not an amount we can assume we’ll get to spend in full. We have 12 volunteers, but only six have said they can stay through cleanup. One volunteer can operate the Cedar Hall equipment; nobody has confirmed that they can operate the union projector. The film runs 82 minutes. We have not settled the event’s start time, whether there will be refreshments, or who will lead the discussion. Please keep open decisions open and don’t treat tentative offers as confirmed bookings.

Some more context that might affect how useful the plan is: The society wants the evening to feel welcoming, but it doesn’t want to promise a discussion format that a facilitator has not agreed to lead. We have a short description of the documentary, and it follows three families responding to the closure of a local orchard. The society’s publicity lead wants to mention that in the event listing but hasn’t written the listing yet. The filmmaker’s recorded introduction is 4 minutes long. It was offered for this screening, but we have not asked whether it can be used in a later event. Keep the recommendation limited to this October screening. Don’t write the event listing, discussion questions, or a message to the filmmaker; those would be separate tasks. One committee member said, “I’d rather have a smaller room that works than promise a huge event we can’t staff.” Another said, “If we can make the auditorium work, more students can come.” Those are two views from the committee, not decisions that have already been made. The prompt should retain both perspectives without choosing one on their behalf.

For the costs, we have the following figures from messages received this week. Cedar Hall has no room charge. The library room has a $35 fee if the late opening is approved. The student union’s auditorium costs $90, with an additional $25 charge if the society needs a union technician. We don’t yet know whether a technician is required or available. Printing 80 simple programs would cost $24, and water and packaged snacks for around 70 attendees are estimated at $55. The estimates for printing and refreshments have not been ordered or paid for. Don’t add these numbers together as though every option and expense applies at once; the room choices are alternatives, and refreshments are undecided. The society has also been told that the library room is reserved for another group until 6:30 p.m. If the library coordinator confirms late opening by Monday, that room could still be considered for the event; if not, don’t present it as available for the screening. We don’t have a comparable opening-time restriction for Cedar Hall or the union auditorium in the information here, so don’t invent one.

1. The immediate job is to recommend which venue to pursue for this screening and what the society should do next. If the information supports more than one viable option, say so rather than pretending there is only one. Compare capacity, confirmed versus unconfirmed availability, equipment readiness, staffing, and the stated costs. The hoped-for attendance is about 70, so explain how that number bears on the room sizes, without saying that 70 people are guaranteed to attend.
2. Include a short event sequence covering arrival, the 82-minute film, the 4-minute recorded introduction, and a possible discussion afterward. We don’t have a start time, so don’t invent clock times or calculate an end time. Address the choice about where the introduction might go, but don’t claim the society has decided. Identify that a discussion lead is not yet confirmed.
3. Keep the spending within the $180 allocation if you discuss a proposed combination of costs, and make clear which items are optional, conditional, or still estimates. For the union option, keep the possible $25 technician charge separate unless the need for a technician is established. Don’t assume that refreshments or printed programs have been approved.

Please make the resulting response a numbered checklist, and make sure each recommendation is preceded by the specific evidence from these notes that supports it. This checklist requirement applies to the response’s recommendations; it doesn’t mean every piece of background has to be turned into an action item. I need something the committee can use at its next meeting, including what to verify before it commits to a room. If the plan depends on the library confirming late opening by Monday, state that condition where it matters. Keep the quoted committee comments as attributed opinions, not as facts about what the whole society wants. The final part should cover the remaining unresolved decisions and the next checks, without giving a made-up final approval or claiming that the room has been booked.", "output": "Create a practical, evidence-based plan for the North Quad Film Society’s screening of the independent documentary *The Last Orchard* on Thursday, October 24. The event is for current students and staff, with hoped-for attendance of about 70 people. The society has permission to screen the film and has received a 4-minute recorded introduction from the filmmaker. Use the information below, keep undecided matters open, and do not assume tentative offers are confirmed. Limit the plan to this October screening; do not write an event listing, discussion questions, or a message to the filmmaker.

**Context and options**

- Cedar Hall 104 seats 64, has a projector and speakers, and has no room charge. The society knows how to use its equipment. One volunteer can operate it.
- The library screening room seats 48 and has better sound. It costs $35 if late opening is approved. Another group has the room until 6:30 p.m. If the library coordinator confirms late opening by Monday, it could still be considered for this event; otherwise, do not present it as available. The coordinator has not confirmed late opening.
- The student union auditorium seats 110 and costs $90. It has a microphone and projector, neither of which the society has tested. The union has not replied about the room. A technician would cost an additional $25 if needed, but whether a technician is required or available is unknown. No opening-time restriction for this room is provided.

The society has up to $180 in its current allocation; this is the total available, not a commitment to spend it all. Printing 80 simple programs is estimated at $24, and water and packaged snacks for around 70 attendees are estimated at $55. Neither expense has been ordered or approved. Refreshments are undecided. Treat the room choices as alternatives and do not combine every listed cost as though it applied at once. Do not assume that refreshments or programs will be purchased.

The society has 12 volunteers, but only six have said they can stay through cleanup. Nobody has confirmed that they can operate the union projector. The film runs 82 minutes. Its description says it follows three families responding to the closure of a local orchard. The publicity lead wants to mention this in an event listing but has not written one. The society has not set a start time, decided whether to serve refreshments, or confirmed a discussion leader. Do not invent a start time or calculate an end time. Do not promise a discussion format that no facilitator has agreed to lead.

The committee has expressed two views: one member said, “I’d rather have a smaller room that works than promise a huge event we can’t staff.” Another said, “If we can make the auditorium work, more students can come.” Treat these as attributed opinions, not decisions or a consensus. The filmmaker’s introduction was offered for this screening; whether it can be used at a later event has not been asked and is outside the scope of this plan.

**Requested plan**

Provide a venue recommendation, including what the society should do next. If more than one option remains viable, say so. Compare capacity with the hoped-for attendance of about 70 without treating attendance as guaranteed. Address availability, equipment readiness, staffing, and the stated costs. Keep any proposed combination of costs within the $180 allocation, and distinguish optional expenses, conditional fees, and estimates. Keep the union’s possible $25 technician fee separate unless the need for a technician is established.

Include a short event sequence covering arrival, the film, the 4-minute recorded introduction, and a possible discussion afterward. Address whether the introduction might go before the film or after it, without claiming that the society has decided. Note that a discussion lead is unconfirmed.

**Output format and final checks**

Return a numbered checklist. Each recommendation must be preceded by the specific evidence from these notes that supports it; the checklist requirement applies to recommendations, not necessarily to every background detail. Make the checklist useful for the committee’s next meeting and include what to verify before committing to a room. State the library’s Monday confirmation condition wherever it affects the plan. End with the unresolved decisions and next checks. Do not claim that a room has been booked, that spending has been approved, or that the society has made a final decision."}]
